questions.q: What is handpicking? When is it used?
questions.a: Picking out unwanted substances by hand, used when impurities are few and large, like pebbles in rice.

questions.q: Give two examples where handpicking works.
questions.a: Removing stones from pulses and pebbles from rice.

questions.q: Why can handpicking not clean flour?
questions.a: The impurities in flour are too small and too many to pick by hand - sieving works better.

questions.q: What is threshing?
questions.a: Separating grain from the stalks by beating, as farmers do after harvest.

questions.q: How is threshing done on a large scale?
questions.a: With machines called threshers that beat the stalks and separate grain quickly.

questions.q: Name the substance separated from stalks by threshing.
questions.a: The grain (like wheat or paddy seeds).

questions.q: What is winnowing?
questions.a: Blowing air on a mixture so the lighter husk blows away and heavier grain falls near.

questions.q: Which property lets winnowing separate husk from grain?
questions.a: Difference in weight - husk is light, grain is heavy.

questions.q: Name the tool used for winnowing.
questions.a: A winnowing basket (soop), tilted against the wind.

questions.q: What is sieving?
questions.a: Passing a mixture through a sieve so fine particles fall through and big ones stay behind.

questions.q: Where is sieving used at home and at construction sites?
questions.a: At home for flour (removing bran); at sites to remove pebbles from sand.

questions.q: When does sieving fail to separate a mixture?
questions.a: When both components are of the same size, or when one is dissolved - other methods are needed.

questions.q: What is sedimentation?
questions.a: Letting an insoluble heavy substance settle at the bottom of a liquid.

questions.q: How does stirring help sedimentation?
questions.a: Stirring in water helps mud loosen and then settle faster at the bottom.

questions.q: Give one example of sedimentation at home.
questions.a: Muddy water in a bucket settling clear at the top after some hours.

questions.q: What is decantation?
questions.a: Pouring off the clear liquid after the heavy particles have settled.

questions.q: How do oil and water separate by decantation?
questions.a: Oil floats on water; the lower water layer is poured out carefully.

questions.q: Name one use of decantation.
questions.a: Pouring clear water from settled mud, or separating water after washing rice.

questions.q: What is filtration?
questions.a: Passing a mixture through a filter (paper, cloth) that holds insoluble solids and lets the liquid pass.

questions.q: Name the liquid that passes through the filter.
questions.a: The filtrate - like clear tea after removing leaves.

questions.q: Give one household and one laboratory use of filtration.
questions.a: Home: filtering tea with a strainer. Lab: filter paper separating chalk from water.

questions.q: What happens during evaporation?
questions.a: A liquid turns into vapour leaving the dissolved solid behind - salt from sea water.

questions.q: How is common salt obtained from sea water?
questions.a: Sea water is spread in shallow beds; the sun evaporates water leaving salt.

questions.q: Why does evaporation recover only the solid, not the liquid?
questions.a: The liquid escapes as vapour into air; only the dissolved solid remains.

questions.q: What is condensation?
questions.a: A vapour cooling back into liquid, as water drops on a cold glass or lid.

questions.q: How can we recover the liquid lost in evaporation?
questions.a: Condense the vapour on a cold surface - as in making potable water by distillation.

questions.q: Give two examples of condensation from daily life.
questions.a: Dew on morning grass and water drops on a mirror after a hot bath.

questions.q: What is a saturated solution?
questions.a: One that has dissolved all the solute it can at that temperature - no more dissolves.

questions.q: How can a saturated sugar solution dissolve more sugar?
questions.a: Warm it - solubility rises with temperature.

questions.q: What happens on cooling a hot saturated solution?
questions.a: Extra solute separates out as crystals.
